abstract.p: Plant height is one of the most critical factors influencing wheat plant architecture, and the application of Green Revolution genes has led to a reduction in plant height and an increase in yield. Discovering new dwarfing genes and alleles can contribute to enhance the genetic diversity of wheat. Here we obtained an EMS induced dwarf wheat mutant je0166 with increased grain weight, which exhibited a reduction in plant height ranging from 46.47% to 49.40%, and its cell length was shorter. The mutant je0166 was sensitive to exogenous gibberellin, but its sensitivity was lower than that of its wild type. Genetic analysis on plant height and gene mapping located the target region to a 4.07 cM interval on chr. 4AL. Within this interval, we identified a co-segregated mutation in Rht-A1h, which is a novel allele of the Green Revolution gene Rht-A1. We also found large fragment inversions in the genetic map of the mutant. The novel allele diversifies natural allelic variations and could be utilized in future wheat improvement. Furthermore, we demonstrated that chemical mutagen treatment led to large fragment inversion.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.) is the third most widely cultivated crop in the world, after rice and maize. As such, enhancing wheat yield remains a major target of wheat breeding (Milach et al. 2001). During the Green Revolution in the 1960s, the introduction of dwarf genes enhanced lodging resistance in crops and boosted grain yields. Dwarfing genes are typically associated with gibberellin (GA) levels, and DELLA proteins act as key repressors in the GA signaling pathway in plants. They regulate plant growth and development by controlling the activity of downstream transcription factors (Hedden 2003). The N-terminus of DELLA proteins contains a specific DELLA/TVHYNP motif, which is a critical recognition site in GA signal transduction. When GA levels rise within plant cells, GA first binds to its receptor GID1, forming the GA-GID1 complex. This complex then specifically interacts with DELLA proteins through the DELLA/TVHYNP motif, forming the GA-GID1-DELLA complex. In the absence of DELLA protein inhibition, GAF1 can activate the expression of genes related to cell elongation, division, and overall plant growth (Pearce et al. 2011). Dwarfing genes can be categorized into GA-responsive and GA-insensitive ones. Rht1, Rht2 and Rht3 belong to the GA-insensitive type, while Rht5, Rht12, Rht4 and Rht8 belong to the GA-responsive category. Rht1 (Rht-B1b), Rht2 (Rht-D1b) and Rht8 are the primary dwarfing genes which have been widely utilized in wheat breeding (Ellis et al. 2002). Rht8 reduces plant height without significant negative effect on thousand grain weight, which enables it to be widely utilized in modern wheat breeding process (Zhou et al. 2023; Jatayev et al. 2020). Meanwhile, Rht-B1b and Rht-D1b also result in negative effects. They lead to shortened coleoptile length and reduced seedling vigor (Li et al. 2011). Therefore, it is important and necessary to identify new dwarf resources for wheat improvement.

Artificial mutagenesis has increased the likelihood of gene mutation in plants (Whittle and Johnston 2006), which can induce new mutant genes or alleles and enrich germplasm resources, including those on plant height (Gillmor and Lukowitz 2020). The alleles of Rht-B1b and Rht-D1b are derived from a gain-of-function mutation of Rht-B1a and Rht-D1a in the B and D subgenomes of wheat, respectively (Guedira et al. 2010). Both alleles are single base-pair changes leading to a TAG stop codon downstream of the start codon (Liu et al. 2021). A newly reported allele of Rht8 is identified via an EMS induced mutant (Zhou et al. 2023). Rht5 is located on chromosome 3B and is induced by EMS mutagenesis in genotype Marfed. It could reduce plant height by 25.84%, increase effective tillers by about 37.39%, and do not significantly affect coleoptile length and seedling vigor (Daoura et al. 2014). The Rht12 gene is dominant to GA treatment, and it is induced by gamma-ray irradiation (Worland et al. 1994). The gene reduces wheat plant height by 46% and has no negative effect on yield (Singh and Balyan 2009; Xu et al. 2017). Rht-NM9 is identified in the dwarf mutant NM9918, which is produced after EMS mutagen treatment. Rht-NM9 reduces plant height and increases effective tiller number, spike length and grain length (Lu et al. 2015), so there is a great potential to uncover more favorable dwarfing alleles from wheat mutant resources.

In this study, a dwarf wheat mutant named je0166 was identified from the winter wheat mutant resource. je0166 exhibited favorable agronomic traits. Its thousand grain weight was increased; the number of spikelets did not reduce significantly although spike length was shorter. We mapped the target gene regulating plant height using a segregation population, which bring new dwarfing allele for wheat improvement.

sec.title: Plant materials
sec.p: The stable dwarf mutant je0166 was identified from the wheat mutant resource induced by ethyl methane sulfonate (EMS) (Guo et al. 2017), and then self-crossed to M6 generation until its phenotype was stable. The winter wheat variety Jing411 is used as the wild type (WT), which do not carry dwarfing alleles/genes Rht-B1b, Rht-D1b or Rht8. The stable dwarf mutant je0166 was hybridized with WT to produce a F2 population (594 individuals) for genetic analysis and gene mapping. The F2 population was expanded to the F2:3 line (594 lines) for phenotypic validation. The population and the parent lines were sown at the Zhongpuchang Station of the Institute of Crop Sciences, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences (Beijing, China), and grown under well-managed field conditions. The F2 population was planted on October 15, 2021, and the F2:3 population was planted on October 1, 2022, each line planted 2 rows with 20 seeds in each row. The row was 2 m long with 20 cm row spacing, and 20 seeds were planted in each row.

sec.title: Phenotypic assessment
sec.p: After harvesting, plant height, internode length, thousand grain weight, spike length and spikelet number of the mutant je0166 and WT were measured or calculated. Plant height was measured from base of stem to top of spike. 100-200 randomly selected grains were measured with an SC-A1 automatic seeds tester (Wseen Technology, China), grain-dimension-related traits and thousand grain weight were calculated. Data between mutant and wild type were assessed with Student’s t test, and those with p < 0.05 or p < 0.01 were considered to be significant or highly significant.

sec.title: Microscopic observation of stem tissue
sec.p: At end of the jointing stage, the 4th internode under spike of the main tiller was collected for cytological observation and measurement. Three biological replicates were set for mutant and WT respectively, and the sampling position was in the middle of the internode. The samples were immediately fixed with 50% FAA fixative (Wang et al. 2022). Observation was performed on a Nikon Eclipse E100 microscope (Nikon Co., Ltd., Tokyo, Japan).

sec.title: Exogenous GA treatment
sec.p: The WT and je0166 were germinated to test their sensitivity to gibberellin. Thirty seeds were randomly selected and put on a bed of moist filter paper on a petri dish with a 12 h light/dark photoperiod cultivation at a temperature of 21 °C. After being cultured with water for 2 days, GA3 solution (2 mg L−1) was added to exogenous gibberellin treatment (Zhou et al. 2020), while the same amount of tap water was added to the control treatment. After a total of eight-day growth, 8 seedlings from each treatment were randomly selected, and lengths of seedling and coleoptile were measured.

sec.title: Bulked segregant analysis and exome capture
sec.p: A Bulked Segregant Analysis (BSA) strategy based on exon capture sequencing was used to map the target gene on plant height, the average read depth of each bulk was up to 20 × , which was conducted in Tcuni Inc. (Chengdu, China). The F2 individuals with extreme plant height were bulked. Two bulks were built for dwarf plant, and the other two were built for tall plant, there were 30 individuals in each bulk. Whole-exome sequencing was conducted on the four bulks and two parental lines using the Illumina HiSeq X platform. Clean reads obtained from sequencing were aligned to the Chinese Spring v2.0 genome of the International Wheat Genome Sequencing Consortium (IWGSC) using the Burrows-Wheeler Aligner (BWA) software. The alignment data were processed into BAM files using SAMtools, and duplicate reads were removed using Biobambam2.

Ten individuals of mutant je0166 were bulked as one of the parents, and sequencing data of the other parent WT came from the Xiong et al. (Xiong et al. 2023). The ΔSNP-index between bulks was calculated to determine the genotypic frequency. To eliminate false positive loci, candidate positions were calculated by locally weighted scatterplot smoothing (LOESS) fitting of the absolute value of the ΔSNP-index (Li et al. 2017).

sec.title: Genotyping with Kompetitive Allele-specific PCR (KASP) marker assay
sec.p: Based on exome capture data, specific SNPs were screened using the following thresholds: Minimum Read Depth was set to 5, SNP Window Size to 20, SNP Step Size to 5, and Allele Frequency Filter [Wild/Mutant, Wild/Mutant Parent or Background] to 0.3. High-confidence SNPs were then used for association analysis with Minimum Read Depth of 5 and Ref Allele Frequency threshold of 0.3, and those with ED values higher than 1 were considered candidate chromosomes. The SNPs on candidate chromosome were selected and designed as KASP markers via the online primer design pipeline PolyMarker (http://polymarker.tgac.ac.uk/). The specificity of KASP markers was tested between parents, and those specific and polymorphic KASP markers (Table S1) were then used to genotype the whole F2 population. KASP assays were performed in 384-well plates following the protocol of LGC Genomics (http://www.lgcgroup.com). A 5.0 µL PCR reaction mixture contained 2.5 µL of 2 × KASP V4.0 master mix, 2.5 µL of genomic DNA (50 ng/µL), and 0.014 µL of primer mix (12 µM of each allele-specific primer and 30 µM of common primer). Thermal cycling programs were 95 °C for 15 min, followed by 9 cycles of touchdown, 95 °C for 20 s, 65 °C for 60 s with decreasing by 0.8 °C per cycle, and then followed by 35 cycles amplification, 95 °C for 20 s, 55 °C for 60 s. The amplifications were conducted on a CFX 96 Real-Time PCR Fluorescence Detection System (Bio Rad, Hercules, CA, USA).

sec.title: Construction of a genetic linkage map
sec.p: A genetic linkage map was constructed using the MAP function of IciMapping V4.2 (Meng et al. 2015). The Kosambi map function was used to convert recombination frequency into centimorgan (cM). The inclusive composite interval mapping (ICIM) analysis was used for QTL mapping. ICIM was used to determine the phenotypic variance (PVE) explained by each QTL. The threshold for significant QTLs was defined with an error of 0.05 and a likelihood of odds (LOD) of 3.0.

sec.title: Identification of Rht-A1
sec.p: Specific primers were designed to amplify the alleles of gene Rht-A1, and forward primer sequence was GCGGGAGATCGAAGTACCA, while the reverse primer sequence was GATAGGTAGAGAAGCGAGGC. PCR was performed using 2 × Phanta®Max Master Mix (Vazyme), and the amplification products were sequenced at BioWorks Biologicals.

sec.title: Wheat mutant je0166 showed decreased plant height
sec.p:
The wheat mutant je0166 exhibited dwarf plant height compared with its WT at maturity stage (Fig. 1a). During the 3 investigated growing seasons, plant height of mutant je0166 was around 45.43 cm, which was 49.40% shorter than that of the WT (Fig. 1a). The mutant had only 4 internodes, and length of each internode was shorter than that of WT (Fig. 1b). The length of peduncle was decreased by 35.27% than that of WT, and the others by 35.82%, 40.64% and 72.18% respectively (Fig. 1b).Fig. 1
Dwarf mutant je0166 and its agronomic traits. a The mutant je0166 and WT under field conditions and their plant height at 3 different growing seasons from 2021 until 2023. b Internode length of the mutant je0166 and WT measured in 2022. c Spike length, number of rachis node and thousand grain weight at 2 different growing seasons from 2021 until 2022. d The cell length of the fourth internode under the spike. Values are average from ten replicates, ** indicates significant differences at 0.01 level

The agronomic traits of the mutant showed significant variation with its WT. Spike length of je0166 was 7.37 cm long, which was 23.31% shorter than that of the WT (Fig. 1c), but no significant variation was observed in rachis nodes or spikelet number (Fig. 1c), while grain numbers per spike were reduced by 7.4%-11.1%; thousand grain weight was 40.65 g, which was 13.31% higher than that of WT (Fig. 1c), and due to the increase of grain area and perimeter but not grain length or width (Fig. S1).

As shown in (Fig. 1a), length of the 4th internode under spike exhibited largest difference between je0166 and WT. Therefore, the cell length of the internode was observed and measured via microscope. The average cell length of mutant je0166 was 155.13 µm, which was shorter by 13.95% than that of the WT (180.27 µm) (Fig. 1d). The results indicate that the cell length of the mutant je0166 was significantly less than that of WT.

sec.title: Mutant je0166 was less sensitive to exogenous gibberellin
sec.p:
Gibberellins (GAs) play a key role in regulating plant height (Bogdan and Doerge 2005). The mutant je0166 and its WT were treated with exogenous gibberellin to test their sensitivity (Fig. 2a). Under the exogenous gibberellin treatment, the seedling length of WT was increased by 67.12%, and the length of its coleoptile by 11.39%; while the seeding length of the mutant je0166 was increased by 26.21% and coleoptile length by 11.39% (Fig. 2b, c). Which means that the mutant je0166 was sensitive to gibberellin, but much less than its WT.Fig. 2
Mutant je0166 was less sensitivity to exogenous gibberellin treatment at seedling stage. a Seedlings of mutant je0166 and WT Jing411 after exogenous GA or CK treatment. b Seedling length. c Coleoptile length. ** indicates significant differences at 0.01 level

sec.title: The dwarf mutation was controlled by a major dominant QTL and located on chr. 4A
sec.p:
Genetic analysis revealed that the F1 plants exhibited dwarfism, being significantly shorter than the WT but taller than the mutant (Fig. 3a). Additionally, the distribution of individual plant heights in the F2 population showed a bimodal pattern (Fig. 3b), indicating that the dwarfism is semi-dominant. The distribution of individual plant heights was like a bimodal mode in the F2 population (Fig. 3b). We deduced that the plant height of the mutant je0166 is controlled by a major QTL.Fig. 3
Plant height distribution and QTL mapping of dwarfing gene in mutant je0166. a Plant height in F1 between mutant and its wild type. b Distribution frequency of plant height in the F2 population derived from mutant and its wild type. c The SNP distribution on chromosomes. d The QTL regulating plant height was mapped on chr. 4A. Green curve was linked with plant height in F2:3, and red curve was linked with those in F2

Based on the exome capture data, a total of 161,044 SNPs were identified between je0166 and WT. After filtering and screening, 66 homozygous differential loci were obtained, with 18 of these being on chr. 4A (Fig. 3c), which should be the candidate region for plant height mutation.

Fifteen KASP markers were successfully developed on chr. 4A. Based on genotyping results, linkage genetic analysis of plant height in the F2 population and F2:3 lines were conducted using IciMapping by 14 markers. In the F2 population, a QTL with a LOD value of 48.48 was detected between markers PhA and Ph13, which explained 53.09% of the phenotypic variation. In the F2:3 lines, a QTL with a LOD value of 61.65 was detected in the same interval, with a phenotypic contribution of 35.42% (Fig. 3d). It was flanked by markers PhA and Ph13 with a genetic distance of 4.07 cM. Therefore, the mutated gene controlling plant height in je0166 was located in the interval between markers PhA and Ph13, which represent the physical positions of 579.21 and 589.13 Mb on the Chinese Spring Reference genome (V2.1) respectively.

sec.title: The novel allelic variation of Rht-A1 conferred the dwarf plant height
sec.p:
Based on the exon capture, only four SNPs were left in the target region. Through alignment with the Chinese Spring V2.1 reference genome, the four SNPs located on four genes (Table S2). Among them, there were three genes that had no relationship with plant height by gene annotations and comparative analysis, however, a known Green Revolution gene, Rht-A1 (TraesCS4A03G0701300), was identified within the 4.07 cM interval. There was a SNP on this gene at 131st based on Sanger sequencing, which was a missense mutation from G to A with the 44th amino acid change from Glu to Gly (Fig. 4). We named the wild type allele as Rht-A1a, and the mutant allele as Rht-A1h. We further verified the missense mutation by sequencing in the F2:3 recombinants, and found that the plant height was co-segregated with it. Recombinants carrying allele Rht-A1a exhibited higher plant heights, those carrying allele Rht-A1h were as short as mutant je0166, and those carrying heterozygous alleles were in between WT and je0166 (Fig. 4), which were aligned with that of F1. So it was the novel allelic variation of Rht-A1 conferring the dwarf plant height, which can reduce plant height by 33.9% based on plant height in recombinants.Fig. 4
Allelic variation of Rht-A1 in mutant and its progenies and their plant heights. a The mutation in je0166 led to variation in Rht-A1 and its amino acid. In the schematic diagram of the Rht-A1h gene structure, the blue rectangle represents the first exon, the green rectangle represents the second exon, the red lines and letters denote the DELLA motif, and the blue lines and letters denote the LEQLE motif. b The mutation in progenies were verified by Sanger sequencing. c Plant height of F2:3 in recombinants of Rht-A1. ** indicates significant differences at 0.01 level

sec.title: EMS mutagenesis caused large fragment inversion
sec.p:
The molecular markers we have developed are based on the Chinese Spring reference genomes (Fig. 5a). The genome of WT has been assembled base on the long-read sequencing by PacBio Sequel II platform (Xiong et al. 2023), and the genetic position of markers on Chr. 4A was identical with those in Chinese Spring (Fig. 5b). However, during the process of genetic map construction of mutant je0166, we found that the large fragment flanked by markers Ph11 and Ph13 has been relocated to the end of short arm, while those flanked by markers Ph1 to Ph4 and beyond have been linked to downstream of Ph11 (Fig. 5c). The mutant je0166 is induced by EMS treatment and selected generation by generation in the field, and the M1 generation after EMS treatment was selfed by isolation bags, there was no possibility of cross pollination, so we deduce that the inversion was caused by chemical treatment.Fig. 5
Large fragment inversions induced by EMS treatment on chr. 4A in wheat. a Physical positions of the developed markers in the Chinese Spring RefSeq V2.1. b Genetic map of Chr. 4A in WT. c Genetic map of Chr. 4A in je0166. Red lines indicate markers that their positions have been changed between mutant and its wild type

sec.title: The mutant carries a novel allelic variation of Rht-A1
sec.p: Landraces and wild relatives have provided abundance genetic variation, and the alleles of Rht-B1, Rht-D1 and other semi-dwarfing genes have been reported. The allele Rht-B1b is caused by the substitution of C with T, resulting in glutamine (Gln, CAG) changing to stop codon (TAA) (Hedden 2003), which results plant height reduction by around 20%. The allele Rht-B1c is due to endogenous insertion, with 90 bases insertions in its transcript (Ellis et al. 2002). The two alleles of Rht-B1d and Rht-B1e are inserted by termination codons in the N-terminal coding region (Pearce et al. 2011). The variation in Rht-D1b is a replacement of G in the codon encoding glutamate (Glu, GAG) with T, which also leads to the appearance of stop codon (TAG) (Hedden 2003). The extreme dwarfism of allele Rht-D1c (Rht10) is caused by multi-copy of Rht-D1b, and the semi dwarf allele Rht-D1b is overexpressed (Thomas 2017). Rht-A1 is the homeologous gene of Rht-B1 and Rht-D1, and their wild types are premature of DELLA proteins (Porotnikov et al. 2022). It has been identified seven alleles of Rht-A1 in natural populations except the wild type Rht-A1a. Unlike Rht-B1b or Rht-D1b, however, all of these alleles have not yet been utilized in modern wheat cultivars up to date. Rht-A1b is the first reported allele (Li et al. 2013). The other 6 reported alleles are from Chinese wheat germplasms. Rht-A1e contains a single SNP in the 5′-non-coding region, Rht-A1b (the same name with the previous one), Rht-A1c, Rht-A1d, and Rht-A1g are located in the functional domains of DELLA proteins, Rht-A1b in the VHIID motif, Rht-A1c in PFYRE, Rht-A1d in LHR1, and Rht-A1g in the Poly S/T/V region (Tang et al. 2021). Our allele Rht-A1h is induced by EMS treatment, which is different from the previous reported natural alleles, and the variation of G131A has not yet been reported. While the dwarfing effect of Rht-A1h is higher than those of the other homoeologous alleles, which needs to be further studied.

The N-terminal DELLA motif, LEQLE motif, and TVHYNP motif are key functional domains of DELLA proteins that respond to gibberellin (GA) signals (Bogdan and Doerge 2005). DELLA and TVHYNP motifs are more important to mediate the interaction between DELLA proteins and GID1 protein, which is a critical step in GA signal transduction pathway (Van De Velde et al. 2021). In non-mutated DELLA proteins, GA binds to the GID1 receptor, which facilitate GID1 to recognize and bind to the TVHYNP motif of DELLA proteins (Ueguchi-Tanaka et al. 2005). This process activates an E3 ubiquitin ligase, which adds ubiquitin to specific lysine residues of the DELLA protein, then ubiquitination chains are formed. Subsequently, the DELLA protein is degraded via the 26S proteasome pathway, thereby its inhibitory effect on plant growth is relieved, and the expressions of growth-promoting genes are recovered. Therefore, plants can finely regulate the stability of DELLA proteins in response to changes in GA levels, achieving precise control over their own growth and development (Murase et al. 2008). The allele Rht-B1c results in the insertion of 30 amino acids in the highly conserved N-terminal DELLA domain (Ellis et al. 2002). Rht-D1b produces truncated proteins at N-terminal, and enhances inhibition of GA signaling and results in semi dwarfing (Hedden 2003). The mutation of Rht-A1h was located within the DELLA motif and at the upstream of those of Rht-B1b or Rht-D1b, while Rht-B1b and Rht-D1b are located within the LEQLE motif, so we deduce that Rht-A1h might lead to more severe effect on the interaction between DELLA and GID1, and result in shorter plant height than other homoeologous alleles, but more experimental evidences are needed to validate it.

sec.title: Dwarf allele has positive pleiotropic effect in thousand grain weight
sec.p: The effects of different Rht genes on plant height are variable. It has demonstrated that Rht-B1b induces a 23% reduction in stem length, while Rht18 and Rht15 exhibit reductions of 7% and 31.5% respectively (Zhang et al. 2013; Zhao et al. 2023). Moreover, Rht12 displays a significant stem reduction effect of 45%, whereas Rht4 demonstrates a notable decrease of 17% (Chen et al.2013). The novel allele Rht-A1h in this study can explain up to 53% plant height variation, and reduce plant height by up to 41.95%, which has greater effects than Rht-B1b, Rht8 and Rht13.

It is reported the Rht genes are pleiotropic on spike length, thousand grain weight and other agronomic traits (Rebetzke et al. 2012). For example, Rht5 increases the effective tillers per plant by 45.77%, while reduces grain number per spike by 13.4% and the grain yield by 15.7% in F2:3 dwarf lines (Cui et al. 2022). Allele Rht-B1b can change grain size and decrease thousand grain weight, individuals carrying the Rht-B1b allele exhibited a 10.1% reduction in grain length and a decrease in individual plant yield of 18.1% compared to the wild type (Hayat et al. 2019). Dwarfing or semi-dwarfing genes used in wheat breeding process have a great role for increasing yield due to enhancements in lodging resistance and harvest index (Shah et al. 2019), the less negative effects would make it more favorable. The mutant je0166 has higher thousand grain weight, which make it to be a favorable allele for yield improvement, but the grain number per spike was reduced by 7.4% to 11.1%, which may have negative effect on yield. However, all of these data were accessed under sparse sowing conditions, large-plot yield trials are necessary to precisely evaluate its effects on yield in future works. The primer sequences can be used for marker assisted selection during breeding process.

sec.title: Chromosome rearrangements occur in crops and result in evolution and variation
sec.p: It has demonstrated that chromosomal rearrangements (CRs) can significantly impact gene expression patterns, metabolic pathways, phenotypes and reveal the origin and domestication of plants (Dvorak et al. 2018). During evolution, ectopic or non-allelic homologous pairing and recombination may occur, and lead to various CRs between non-homologous chromosomes (Walkowiak et al. 2020). New CRs event is sufficient to induce dysregulation of hundreds to thousands of genes with variable extents between tissues in a synthetic hexaploid wheat (Marcussen et al. 2014). Banana is derived from Musa acuminata through six large chromosomal translocations (Martin et al. 2020). The translocation induces differentially expressed genes, which are functionally relevant and can lead to beneficial variations in both metabolome and morphological/physiological phenotypes (Wang et al.2021). In maize, enhancer KRN4 is located at 33.1 to 49.9 kb downstream of gene UB3, after chromatin folding, KRN4 could spatially interact with the promoter of UB3, which affect UB3 expression and hence regulate inflorescence development (Du et al.2020). We discovered the large fragment inversions induced by EMS treatment, although it has not obvious impact on plant height, which might contribute to other phenotypic variations, and it needs further in-depth investigation and research efforts. It also demonstrated that EMS mutagen not only induce single and/or small base variations, but also large fragment mutation.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: In this study, plant height of the mutant was reduced due to reduction of internode and cell lengths, it was less sensitive to exogenous gibberellin. The mutation of plant height was controlled by a major QTL on chr. 4A, and co-segregated with gene Rht-A1. The novel allele Rht-A1h was a missense mutation G131A, which has a great potential to be used for wheat improvement. We also demonstrated that EMS can induce large fragment inversion.
